newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea arrests Hanbo founder, tries to rescue firm.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea arrests Hanbo founder, tries to rescue firm.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors Friday arrested Chung Tae-soo, founder of the stricken Hanbo Group, while the government took steps to rescue the conglomerate's flagship steel-making unit.
One prosecutor said the head of the nation's 14th-biggest conglomerate was charged with fraud, illegally issuing checks and violating the law on mutual trust and savings companies.
Chung's arrest was broadcast live at prime time by state television.
The arrest was made at the prosecutors' office where Chung had been questioned about massive loans to shaky Hanbo Steel Co. since being summoned from a Seoul hospital on Thursday.
The prosecutor said investigations would not be limited to the charges but would cover "all suspicions and allegations" about Chung.

Prosecutors accused Chung of continuing to issue promissory notes even after he knew that Hanbo faced insolvency. He was also accused of illegally withdrawing loans from the Hanbo Group's trust and savings unit.
"But the main focus of investigation would be on loans from Hanbo Steel's creditor banks," one prosecution source said. "Chung will also be questioned if he bribed anybody to secure the loans."
Chung has not commented on any of the charges.
Hanbo Steel, the nation's second-biggest steelmaker, defaulted on debt repayments last week after piling up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions.
Government officials said although Chung must face justice for any illegal activity, the steel company would be rescued to control the shock to the economy.

Finance and Economy Minister Han Seung-soo reported to President Kim Young-sam that about 100 billion won ($116 million) would be set aside to keep Hanbo Steel running and to help the company's suppliers weather Hanbo's problems.
At a meeting between Kim and his top economic officials, Han said the emergency fund would help Hanbo pay for raw materials and transport costs, according to ministry officials.

Kim said Hanbo's failure, which followed nearly a month of nationwide labour strife, posed further difficulties to the already slowing economy and that the government should make sure Hanbo Steel remained operational, his spokesman said.
Han said a buyer could be found once Hanbo Steel finished building its new mill, which has an annual capacity of six million tons, later this year.
A Seoul court said on Friday it had decided to freeze Hanbo Steel's assets until a decision was made on the company's request for receivership.
President Kim, who ordered a thorough probe into the loans on Monday, said the crisis appeared to stem from Hanbo Steel's heavy reliance on borrowing to fund excessive expansion.
